note: Peer-reviewed research behind Abide's Science entries. Every paper's metadata was checked against the publisher, Crossref or a repository; 'found' and 'limits' are written in our own words. strength: strong, moderate, early, contested or null.

li-2016.authors: Li S, Stampfer MJ, Williams DR, VanderWeele TJ
li-2016.title: Association of Religious Service Attendance With Mortality Among Women
li-2016.design: Prospective cohort (Nurses' Health Study), 74,534 US women free of cardiovascular disease and cancer at baseline; attendance reported 1992 and 1996, mortality followed 1996-2012; 13,537 deaths
li-2016.found: Women attending religious services more than once a week had a lower death rate over follow-up than women who never attended (all-cause HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62-0.71), with a dose-response pattern (p for trend <0.0001). Cardiovascular mortality HR 0.73 (0.62-0.85); cancer mortality HR 0.79 (0.70-0.89). Social support, depressive symptoms, smoking and optimism partly explained the association.
li-2016.limits: Observational, so cannot prove cause; healthier people may be more able to attend (reverse causation), though baseline illness was excluded and many confounders adjusted. Mostly white Christian US nurses of similar socioeconomic status, as the authors themselves note.

vanderweele-2016.authors: VanderWeele TJ, Li S, Tsai AC, Kawachi I
vanderweele-2016.title: Association Between Religious Service Attendance and Lower Suicide Rates Among US Women
vanderweele-2016.design: Prospective cohort (Nurses' Health Study), 89,708 US women, followed 1996 to June 2010; 36 suicides
vanderweele-2016.found: Women attending services at least weekly had a markedly lower suicide rate than those who never attended (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46), roughly five-fold lower, after adjusting for demographics, lifestyle, medical history, depressive symptoms and social integration. Among Catholics the HR was 0.05 (0.006-0.48) versus 0.34 (0.10-1.10) among Protestants (comparing weekly or more with less frequent attendance).
vanderweele-2016.limits: Only 36 suicides, so estimates are imprecise (wide confidence intervals; the Protestant estimate is not statistically significant). Observational; the authors note possible unmeasured confounding by personality, impulsivity or hopelessness, and a sample of mainly white Christian US female nurses.

chen-2018.title: Associations of Religious Upbringing With Subsequent Health and Well-Being From Adolescence to Young Adulthood: An Outcome-Wide Analysis
chen-2018.design: Prospective cohort (Growing Up Today Study, children of Nurses' Health Study II mothers); 5,681 to 7,458 participants depending on outcome; mean baseline age 14.7; 8-14 years of follow-up (1999 to 2007, 2010 or 2013); many outcomes, Bonferroni-corrected
chen-2018.found: Compared with no attendance, attending religious services at least weekly in adolescence was associated with greater life satisfaction and positive affect in young adulthood, several character strengths (e.g. volunteering), and lower probabilities of marijuana use and early sexual initiation and fewer lifetime sexual partners. Weekly attendance was also associated with slightly fewer depressive symptoms (-0.12, 95% CI -0.19 to -0.04). The press release summarises it as about 18% more likely to report higher happiness and 33% less likely to use illicit drugs.
chen-2018.limits: Observational; religious upbringing travels with family factors that are hard to fully measure. Sample was mainly children of white, relatively high socioeconomic status US mothers; effects on many outcomes were modest and some did not survive multiple-testing correction.

vanderweele-2025.authors: VanderWeele TJ, Johnson BR, Bialowolski PT, et al. (51 authors)
vanderweele-2025.title: The Global Flourishing Study: Study Profile and Initial Results on Flourishing
vanderweele-2025.design: Wave 1 of a planned 5-year longitudinal panel; 202,898 adults in 22 countries on six continents, nationally representative sampling; these first results are cross-sectional, plus retrospective reports of childhood (age 12)
vanderweele-2025.found: Meta-analysed across countries, mean flourishing (0-10 scale) ranged from 6.86 among people who never attend religious services to 7.67 among those attending more than weekly; frequent attenders reported higher flourishing in every country, but the gap ranged from 2.33 (2.12-2.54) in Hong Kong to 0.15 (-0.01 to 0.30) in India. Weekly attendance at age 12 (recalled) was linked with somewhat higher adult flourishing (0.27, 95% CI 0.17-0.36), largest in Poland (1.02), with slightly negative estimates in Kenya, South Africa and Tanzania.
vanderweele-2025.limits: The authors state the demographic analyses are purely descriptive and should not be interpreted causally; childhood data are retrospective and subject to recall bias. Only wave 1, so it cannot yet show change over time; the size of the link varies a lot by country.

holtlunstad-2010.authors: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB
holtlunstad-2010.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
holtlunstad-2010.design: Meta-analysis of 148 prospective studies, 308,849 participants, average follow-up 7.5 years
holtlunstad-2010.found: People with stronger social relationships had about 50% greater likelihood of survival over follow-up (OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.42-1.59). Complex measures of social integration showed the strongest association (OR 1.91, 1.63-2.23). It is not a study of religion, but it shows that social connection, one of the main things a congregation offers, is itself strongly tied to survival.
holtlunstad-2010.limits: Pools observational studies of varying quality and measures, so it cannot establish cause and is open to confounding and reverse causation (sick people may withdraw socially). Says nothing about religion directly; it is relevant as a likely pathway, and it suggests some 'religion' effects may be community effects.

sloan-1999.authors: Sloan RP, Bagiella E, Powell T
sloan-1999.title: Religion, spirituality, and medicine
sloan-1999.design: Critical review/viewpoint essay assessing the evidence base, not an empirical study
sloan-1999.found: Argued the evidence for a religion-health link was 'weak and inconsistent': many studies failed to adjust for confounders such as age, sex, education, socioeconomic status and functional capacity (very ill people cannot get to church), tested many religion and health measures so that some correlated by chance, and defined religion inconsistently. Also argued on ethical grounds that doctors should not recommend religious practice, and that implying faith brings health could leave sick patients feeling guilty.
sloan-1999.limits: Written before the larger, better-adjusted prospective cohorts (such as the Nurses' Health Study analyses), which address several of its methodological points; its ethical argument stands independently of the data.

benson-2006.authors: Benson H, Dusek JA, Sherwood JB, Lam P, Bethea CF, Carpenter W, Levitsky S, Hill PC, Clem DW, Jain MK, Drumel D, Kopecky SL, Mueller PS, Marek D, Rollins S, Hibberd PL
benson-2006.title: Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (STEP) in cardiac bypass patients: a multicenter randomized trial of uncertainty and certainty of receiving intercessory prayer
benson-2006.design: Randomised controlled trial, 1,802 coronary bypass patients at 6 US hospitals, three groups (604 prayed for and told they might be; 597 not prayed for and told they might be; 601 prayed for and told they would be)
benson-2006.found: Being prayed for by strangers made no difference: complications in 52% (315/604) of those who received prayer versus 51% (304/597) of those who did not (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.92-1.15). Patients told for certain they would be prayed for had more complications, 59% (352/601) versus 52% (RR 1.14, 1.02-1.28).
benson-2006.limits: Tests distant intercessory prayer by strangers, not a person's own faith, practice or community, so it says nothing about religious attendance. The excess complications in the 'certain' group may be chance or anxiety and should not be overinterpreted; many theologians also question whether prayer can or should be tested this way.

stavrova-2015.title: Religion, self-rated health, and mortality: Whether religiosity delays death depends on the cultural context
stavrova-2015.design: Two observational studies: Study 1, cross-national survey data from 59 countries; Study 2, US data on self-rated health and mortality by regional level of religiosity
stavrova-2015.found: The positive association between religiosity and self-rated health was 'an exception found in a relatively small number of countries': it appeared mainly where religiosity is a social norm. Within the US, the links with better self-rated health and lower mortality largely depended on how religious the region was, suggesting the benefits are restricted to highly religious regions.
stavrova-2015.limits: Observational and largely cross-sectional for health (self-rated rather than measured); a single-author study whose 'person-culture fit' explanation is one interpretation among others. It is a counterweight, not a refutation, and the Global Flourishing Study later found attendance linked with flourishing even in secular countries.

lally-2010.authors: Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J
lally-2010.title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
lally-2010.design: 96 volunteers chose one new daily eating, drinking or activity behaviour in a consistent context and self-reported its automaticity daily for 12 weeks; individual non-linear (asymptotic) curves were fitted.
lally-2010.found: Automaticity rose along an asymptotic curve: quickly at first, then levelling off. Time to reach 95% of each person's plateau ranged from 18 to 254 days, with a median of 66 days. Missing a single opportunity did not materially disrupt habit formation, although many missed repetitions had a cumulative effect.
lally-2010.limits: Of 96 recruited, 82 gave enough data and the curve fitted well for only 39, so the 66-day median rests on under half the sample; 254 days is an extrapolation beyond the 84-day study. Automaticity was self-reported, and the behaviours were simple health habits chosen by students and staff.

singh-2024.authors: Singh B, Murphy A, Maher C, Smith AE
singh-2024.title: Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants
singh-2024.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (2,601 participants) on forming health-behaviour habits.
singh-2024.found: Only four studies reported time to habit formation: medians of 59-66 days and means of 106-154 days, with very wide individual variation (4-335 days). Across interventions, habit strength rose pre- to post-intervention (standardised mean difference 0.69, 95% CI 0.49-0.88).
singh-2024.limits: Few studies measured time to habit at all, and the pre-post pooled effect is not a controlled comparison. Health behaviours, not spiritual or reflective practices, were studied.

karl-2018.title: Rituals, Repetitiveness and Cognitive Load: A Competitive Test of Ritual Benefits for Stress
karl-2018.design: Pre-registered experiment (osf.io/rsu9x): 180 undergraduates given a stress or control induction, then assigned to control, cognitive load, undirected movement, movement plus cognitive load, or a ritualistic task; self-report and continuous physiological measures.
karl-2018.found: The authors 'failed to find direct support' for ritual reducing anxiety through cognitive load. Induced stress did increase people's spontaneous repetitive behaviour, which in turn was associated with lower physiological arousal.
karl-2018.limits: One student sample with a lab-invented ritual, not a meaningful religious one; the positive finding is a mediation pathway, not a randomised effect of ritual.

emmons-2003.title: Counting blessings versus burdens: an experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being in daily life
emmons-2003.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
emmons-2003.design: Three randomised studies: weekly (Study 1, 192 undergraduates) and daily (Study 2, 157 undergraduates) records after listing blessings vs hassles vs neutral events or downward social comparison; Study 3, 65 adults with neuromuscular disease, gratitude vs control for about three weeks.
emmons-2003.found: Gratitude groups showed higher well-being on several, though not all, outcome measures relative to comparison groups. The effect on positive affect was the most robust finding.
emmons-2003.limits: Small samples, mostly students, self-report outcomes, and comparisons against 'hassles' lists (which may make people feel worse) can inflate the apparent gratitude benefit. Later meta-analyses find much smaller effects.

davis-2016.authors: Davis DE, Choe E, Meyers J, Wade N, Varjas K, Gifford A, Quinn A, Hook JN, Van Tongeren DR, Griffin BJ, Worthington EL Jr
davis-2016.title: Thankful for the little things: A meta-analysis of gratitude interventions
davis-2016.design: Meta-analysis of randomised gratitude interventions (ks 4-18; Ns 395-1,755 per comparison) against measurement-only, alternative-activity and psychologically active comparison conditions.
davis-2016.found: Against measurement-only controls, psychological well-being improved (d = .31, k = 5). Against alternative activities, the effect on well-being was small (d = .17, k = 20) and on anxiety not significant (d = .11). Against psychologically active comparisons, there was no difference (d = .03, k = 9); the authors call the evidence 'positive but limited'.
davis-2016.limits: Few studies per comparison, mostly short and with student samples; the effect shrinks as the comparison gets more credible, which suggests expectancy and attention explain part of it.

cregg-2021.title: Gratitude Interventions: Effective Self-help? A Meta-analysis of the Impact on Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety
cregg-2021.design: Meta-analysis of 27 studies (3,675 participants) of gratitude interventions measuring depression and anxiety symptoms.
cregg-2021.found: Gratitude interventions had a small effect on depression and anxiety symptoms at post-test (g = -0.29) and follow-up (g = -0.23). Effects were larger against waitlist than active controls, and the authors advise people with depression or anxiety to use interventions with stronger evidence.
cregg-2021.limits: Mostly non-clinical samples and short interventions; the waitlist-control advantage again points to non-specific effects.

pennebaker-1997.title: Writing About Emotional Experiences as a Therapeutic Process
pennebaker-1997.design: Short review by the originator of the expressive-writing paradigm: people randomly assigned to write about deeply personal emotional topics, or superficial ones, for 15-30 minutes on 3-5 consecutive days.
pennebaker-1997.found: Reports that emotional writing has been followed by physical and mental health improvements (e.g. fewer physician visits, some immune markers, grades, faster re-employment after layoff). Proposes that changes in cognitive and linguistic processing during writing, more than release of inhibition, predict benefit.
pennebaker-1997.limits: A review largely of the author's own lab's early studies; it notes few reliable changes in health behaviours. Later meta-analyses show the average effect is small.

frattaroli-2006.title: Experimental disclosure and its moderators: a meta-analysis
frattaroli-2006.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of 146 randomised studies of experimental disclosure (mostly expressive writing).
frattaroli-2006.found: Disclosure was effective on average, but the effect was small: r = .075 (95% CI .052-.098). A number of moderators were identified (for example, features of the writing procedure and of participants).
frattaroli-2006.limits: An r of .075 is about d = 0.15, small for any one person; heterogeneity is large and many outcomes are self-reported. Several later trials in clinical groups found null results.

wade-2014.authors: Wade NG, Hoyt WT, Kidwell JEM, Worthington EL Jr
wade-2014.title: Efficacy of psychotherapeutic interventions to promote forgiveness: A meta-analysis
wade-2014.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
wade-2014.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of 54 reports: 53 post-treatment effect sizes (N = 2,323) and 41 follow-up effect sizes (N = 1,716) for professionally delivered interventions explicitly aimed at forgiving a specific hurt.
wade-2014.found: Forgiveness treatments produced more forgiveness than no treatment (delta = 0.56 [0.43, 0.68]) and than alternative treatments (delta = 0.45 [0.21, 0.69]), and larger changes in depression, anxiety and hope than no treatment. Longer interventions and individual (rather than group) delivery uniquely predicted larger gains.
wade-2014.limits: These are guided therapeutic programmes, not brief self-help; the mental-health benefits were shown against no-treatment rather than active controls, and the main outcome (forgiveness) is self-reported. Several authors developed the interventions studied.

goyal-2014.authors: Goyal M, Singh S, Sibinga EMS, et al.
goyal-2014.title: Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis
goyal-2014.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials with active controls: 47 trials, 3,515 participants (from 18,753 citations), with evidence graded for risk of bias, precision, directness and consistency.
goyal-2014.found: Mindfulness programmes had moderate evidence of improving anxiety (effect size 0.38 at 8 weeks; 0.22 at 3-6 months), depression (0.30; 0.23) and pain (0.33), and low evidence for stress/distress and mental-health quality of life. There was low or insufficient evidence for positive mood, attention, substance use, eating, sleep and weight, and no evidence that meditation beat other active treatments.
goyal-2014.limits: Clinical populations and structured programmes (typically 8 weeks), not a few minutes of daily silence; trials up to November 2012.

borde-2003.authors: Borde A, Guth AH, Vilenkin A
borde-2003.title: Inflationary Spacetimes Are Incomplete in Past Directions
borde-2003.found: The paper proves that any spacetime whose expansion rate, averaged along a past-directed path, stays above zero cannot be extended indefinitely into the past. So an inflating universe cannot have been inflating forever, and some other physics must describe its past boundary.
borde-2003.limits: The theorem says the past is incomplete under its assumptions. It does not show that time or the universe had an absolute beginning, and it does not say what lies at the boundary. Models that break its averaged-expansion condition (cyclic, 'emergent' or bouncing models), or quantum-gravity effects, can avoid it, and later work (e.g. Kinney, Maity & Sriramkumar 2024, Phys Rev D 109:043519) examines where it applies. Vilenkin reads it as pointing to a beginning; other physicists, Guth included, are more cautious.

carter-1974.title: Large Number Coincidences and the Anthropic Principle in Cosmology
carter-1974.journal: In: Longair MS (ed.), Confrontation of Cosmological Theories with Observational Data, IAU Symposium 63 (Dordrecht: Reidel), pp. 291–298
carter-1974.found: Carter coins the 'anthropic principle'. In its weak form it says that what we can observe must be compatible with our existence as observers, which explains certain numerical coincidences in physics without special design. He also states a stronger form about the constants of nature, and links it to the idea of an ensemble of universes.
carter-1974.limits: It is a principle about selection effects, not an explanation of why a life-permitting universe exists at all. Critics say the strong form is either trivial or untestable. Theists and atheists both cite it, for opposite conclusions. Note: the same paper also has a Springer chapter DOI (10.1007/978-94-010-2220-0_25) and was reprinted in Gen Rel Grav 43:3225 (2011).

weinberg-1987.title: Anthropic Bound on the Cosmological Constant
weinberg-1987.found: Weinberg argues that if the cosmological constant varies across regions or universes, observers can only exist where it is small enough for galaxies to form. He sets an upper limit, roughly a few hundred times the present matter density. The cosmological constant measured in 1998 is small and positive, in line with this style of reasoning.
weinberg-1987.limits: This is the leading example of using the multiverse plus selection effects to explain a fine-tuned value without a designer. It depends on assuming such an ensemble exists and on a probability measure across it, which remains contested. Weinberg, an atheist, saw it as an alternative to design, not as support for it.

barnes-2012.title: The Fine-Tuning of the Universe for Intelligent Life
barnes-2012.journal: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia
barnes-2012.found: Barnes surveys the physics literature on how much the constants, the initial conditions and even the form of the laws could change before complex structure (stable atoms, stars, chemistry) became impossible. He concludes that fine-tuning is a real feature of current physics. He also rebuts Victor Stenger's claim, in his 2011 book The Fallacy of Fine-Tuning, that it is an illusion.
barnes-2012.limits: Barnes argues that fine-tuning is real but does not argue that it proves design. He treats design, a multiverse and a deeper physical law as candidate explanations. Critics note that the probability measures for 'how likely' a constant is are not well defined (the normalisation problem), and that results depend on which parameters are varied together.

adams-2019.title: The degree of fine-tuning in our universe — and others
adams-2019.found: Adams works through how far each constant could be changed while still allowing stars, nucleosynthesis, planets and structure. He finds that many constants can vary by large factors, sometimes orders of magnitude, if others change with them. He argues that our universe is not maximally fine-tuned, and that some alternative universes could be more hospitable to life.
adams-2019.limits: The paper weakens the strongest claims of 'knife-edge' tuning, but it still finds some constraints are real. It does not settle why the constants fall in the life-permitting range at all. Defenders of fine-tuning reply that a wider life-permitting range still sits within a much larger possible range.

wigner-1960.title: The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences. Richard Courant lecture in mathematical sciences delivered at New York University, May 11, 1959
wigner-1960.journal: Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics
wigner-1960.found: Wigner, a Nobel physicist, argues that mathematics developed for its own beauty turns out, again and again, to describe nature with startling precision. He calls this 'a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve' and says it has no rational explanation.
wigner-1960.limits: It is a reflective essay, not an argument for God, and Wigner draws no theological conclusion. Critics (e.g. Hamming 1980) suggest selection effects instead: we choose the mathematics that works and notice the successes, and much of nature resists neat mathematical description.

nagel-1974.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
nagel-1974.found: Nagel argues that an organism is conscious if there is 'something it is like' to be it. That subjective character cannot be captured by any objective, physical description, however complete. We might know all about a bat's echolocation and still not know what it is like for the bat.
nagel-1974.limits: Nagel does not argue for a soul or against physicalism as such. He says only that we currently lack the concepts to see how physicalism could be true. Physicalists reply that a gap in our concepts is not a gap in reality (the 'phenomenal concept strategy').

chalmers-1995.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness
chalmers-1995.found: Chalmers separates the 'easy problems' (explaining the brain functions of discrimination, report and attention) from the 'hard problem': why any of that processing is accompanied by experience at all. He argues that reductive explanation cannot close the gap. He proposes a non-reductive naturalism, with experience as a fundamental feature tied to information.
chalmers-1995.limits: Chalmers is a naturalist, not a theist, and his view does not imply a soul. Critics (Dennett, Churchland, the illusionists) deny that there is a further hard problem once the functions are explained.

libet-1983.authors: Libet B, Gleason CA, Wright EW, Pearl DK
libet-1983.title: Time of conscious intention to act in relation to onset of cerebral activity (readiness-potential): the unconscious initiation of a freely voluntary act
libet-1983.design: EEG experiment with a very small sample (a small number of participants) making spontaneous wrist flexions and reporting, via a clock, when they first felt the urge
libet-1983.found: The readiness potential, a slow build-up of brain activity, began several hundred milliseconds before people reported being aware of wanting to move. This was widely read as showing that the brain 'decides' before we consciously do.
libet-1983.limits: Libet himself held that consciousness could still veto an action. The task (an arbitrary flick of the wrist with no reason behind it) tells us little about deliberate choices, and the timing reports are open to measurement error. Later work (Schurger et al. 2012) challenges what the readiness potential means.

schurger-2012.authors: Schurger A, Sitt JD, Dehaene S
schurger-2012.title: An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement
schurger-2012.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA
schurger-2012.design: Computational model plus EEG experiment (Libet-style task with unpredictable interruptions)
schurger-2012.found: The authors show that the readiness potential can arise when spontaneous, random fluctuations in neural activity happen to cross a threshold. Averaging activity backwards from the moment of movement then makes it look like a gradual build-up. On this view, the ramp is not an unconscious decision already made. Their EEG data fit the model's predictions.
schurger-2012.limits: The paper removes the strongest 'the brain decided first' reading of Libet. It does not prove that conscious will causes action, and it says nothing about souls. It is about when arbitrary movements happen, not about how meaningful choices are made.

frankish-2016.title: Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness
frankish-2016.design: Philosophical argument (target article with about 20 invited responses in the same issue)
frankish-2016.found: Frankish argues that phenomenal consciousness, as usually conceived, is an illusion. Our brains misrepresent their own states as having special qualitative properties. So the task is to explain why we believe in such properties (the 'illusion problem'), not to explain the properties themselves. This is the strongest scientific-materialist reply to Nagel and Chalmers.
frankish-2016.limits: Critics (e.g. in the same issue, and Strawson) say the view is self-undermining: an illusion is itself something experienced, so experience cannot be an illusion. Illusionism is a minority position, but it is taken seriously, and it shows that 'consciousness proves the soul' is not a scientific conclusion.

keltner-2003.title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
keltner-2003.design: Theoretical review (prototype analysis); no new data
keltner-2003.found: The authors define awe by two features: perceived vastness, and a need for accommodation (one's mental frameworks have to stretch to take something in). They trace its roots in religious, political and aesthetic writing and propose a research agenda. This paper founded the modern psychology of awe.
keltner-2003.limits: It is a conceptual framework, not evidence of effects. Its claims about what awe does were left for later studies to test.

rudd-2012.authors: Rudd M, Vohs KD, Aaker J
rudd-2012.title: Awe expands people's perception of time, alters decision making, and enhances well-being
rudd-2012.design: 3 experiments, N = 63, 86 and 105 (students and an online panel); awe induced by video, recalled memory or a story
rudd-2012.found: Compared with happiness or a neutral state, induced awe made people feel they had more time and made them less impatient. It also raised their willingness to volunteer time, their preference for experiences over goods and, in one study, their reported life satisfaction in that moment.
rudd-2012.limits: Samples are small and the p-values sit close to .05 (e.g. p = .01–.03). These are short-lived self-reports straight after the induction, typical of pre-2015 social psychology. We found no large preregistered replication, so treat the findings as early.

piff-2015.authors: Piff PK, Dietze P, Feinberg M, Stancato DM, Keltner D
piff-2015.title: Awe, the small self, and prosocial behavior
piff-2015.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
piff-2015.design: 5 studies, total N = 2,078 (a correlational survey plus experiments, including standing among tall eucalyptus trees vs looking at a building)
piff-2015.found: People who feel awe more often, and people induced to feel awe, behaved more generously and ethically in lab tasks (e.g. sharing, helping). The effect was partly explained by a 'small self', a sense of personal smallness relative to something vast.
piff-2015.limits: The outcomes are brief lab measures of helping, not real-world behaviour over time, and some individual effects are modest. The paper has comments on PubPeer. No large preregistered multi-lab replication was found.

lin-2025.authors: Lin R, Yu Q, Hu T, Zhang J, Ye Y, Lian R
lin-2025.title: The relationship between awe and prosocial behavior: Three-level meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling
lin-2025.design: Meta-analysis: 221 correlational studies (620 effect sizes) and 152 experimental studies
lin-2025.found: Across studies, awe is positively linked with prosocial behaviour. The pooled correlation is about r = 0.37, and induced awe has an average effect of about g = 0.59.
lin-2025.limits: An average effect this large is unusual for brief emotion inductions, which is a warning sign of small-study and publication bias. We could not confirm from the accessible pages how the authors corrected for that bias. The journal publishes mainly in Chinese, with English abstracts. A 2024 meta-analysis (Li et al., Current Psychology 43:24702–24711, doi 10.1007/s12144-024-06039-9; 57 effect sizes, N = 20,997) also finds a moderate positive link, mostly from correlational data.

lemaitre-1931.title: The Beginning of the World from the Point of View of Quantum Theory
lemaitre-1931.found: Lemaître proposes that the expanding universe began from a single quantum, a highly concentrated initial state that broke up, so that space and time only acquire meaning once that state has divided. This is the seed of what became Big Bang cosmology, and it was written by a Catholic priest who was also a physicist.
lemaitre-1931.limits: It is a short speculative letter, not a worked-out model. Lemaître himself kept his cosmology apart from the doctrine of creation and objected when it was presented as proof of it. Modern cosmology confirms a hot, dense early phase but leaves open whether that phase was an absolute beginning.

white-2019.authors: White CA, Uttl B, Holder MD
white-2019.title: Meta-analyses of positive psychology interventions: The effects are much smaller than previously reported
white-2019.design: Re-analysis and replication of two highly cited meta-analyses of positive psychology interventions (Sin and Lyubomirsky 2009; Bolier et al. 2013), extracting effect sizes from the primary studies and correcting for small-sample bias.
white-2019.found: The earlier meta-analyses had reported effects on well-being of r = .29 and r = .17 (subjective) or .10 (psychological), and on depression of r = .31 and r = .11. Many primary studies were small, and small-sample bias was pronounced. Once it was taken into account, the effect on well-being was small but significant (about r = .10), while effects on depression were variable, dependent on outliers and generally not statistically significant.
white-2019.limits: A re-analysis of existing studies, not new data. Positive psychology interventions are a mixed group (gratitude, kindness, strengths exercises and others), so it says little about any single practice; a small average effect can still matter for some people or over long periods.

brown-2013.authors: Brown NJL, Sokal AD, Friedman HL
brown-2013.title: The complex dynamics of wishful thinking: The critical positivity ratio
brown-2013.design: Critical re-examination of Fredrickson and Losada (2005), which used equations from fluid dynamics to claim that people flourish when positive emotions outnumber negative ones by at least 2.9013 to 1.
brown-2013.found: The authors found no theoretical or empirical justification for applying fluid-dynamics equations to human emotions, and numerous fundamental conceptual and mathematical errors in how they were applied. They concluded that the claim of a critical minimum positivity ratio of 2.9013 is 'entirely unfounded'.
brown-2013.limits: It refutes one widely popularised claim, not the study of positive emotion as a whole: it does not show that positive emotions are unimportant to well-being. It is a critique of method, not a new empirical study.

tedeschi-2004.title: Posttraumatic Growth: Conceptual Foundations and Empirical Evidence
tedeschi-2004.design: Theoretical target article and narrative review by the researchers who named the field, proposing a model of how positive change can arise from the struggle with a major life crisis.
tedeschi-2004.found: Defines posttraumatic growth as positive change experienced as a result of the struggle with highly challenging crises, seen as greater appreciation of life, more meaningful relationships, a sense of personal strength, changed priorities and a richer spiritual life. Reports that accounts of growth after trauma far outnumber reports of psychiatric disorder, while warning that growth should not be expected as an inevitable result.
tedeschi-2004.limits: A conceptual review, not a new study; the evidence it draws on is largely retrospective self-report, in which people rate how much they think they have changed. Later prospective work (Frazier et al. 2009) questions whether such reports reflect real change.

frazier-2009.authors: Frazier P, Tennen H, Gavian M, Park C, Tomich P, Tashiro T
frazier-2009.title: Does Self-Reported Posttraumatic Growth Reflect Genuine Positive Change?
frazier-2009.design: Prospective study: undergraduates completed measures of the usual growth domains, then again two months later. The 122 who experienced a traumatic event in between also completed the Posttraumatic Growth Inventory, so reported growth could be compared with measured change.
frazier-2009.found: Self-reported growth was generally unrelated to actual change in the growth domains. Perceived growth went with increased distress from before to after the trauma, whereas actual growth went with decreased distress; perceived (but not actual) growth was linked to coping by positive reinterpretation. The authors conclude that retrospective growth measures do not appear to measure actual change.
frazier-2009.limits: A single student sample followed for only two months; it challenges how growth is measured rather than showing that genuine growth never happens.

lambert-2010.authors: Lambert NM, Fincham FD, Stillman TF, Graham SM, Beach SRH
lambert-2010.title: Motivating Change in Relationships: Can Prayer Increase Forgiveness?
lambert-2010.design: Two small randomised experiments. Study 1 (N = 52): participants prayed for their romantic partner or described their partner to an imagined parent. Study 2 (N = 67): participants prayed for a friend, prayed about any topic, or thought positive thoughts about a friend, every day for 4 weeks.
lambert-2010.found: In Study 1, those who prayed for their partner reported greater willingness to forgive the partner. In Study 2, those who prayed for their friend reported more forgiveness of that friend than either comparison group, even controlling for baseline forgiveness; they also grew in selfless concern, which statistically accounted for the increase in forgiveness.
lambert-2010.limits: Small samples from the authors' own research programme; forgiveness was self-reported and followed for weeks, not months. It tests whether praying changes the person who prays, not whether prayer influences anything beyond them, and larger independent replications are lacking.

dai-2014.authors: Dai H, Milkman KL, Riis J
dai-2014.title: The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior
dai-2014.design: Three archival field studies: Google searches for 'diet', daily gym attendance records at a university, and goal commitments made on a commitment-contract website, each analysed around temporal landmarks such as the start of a week, month, year or semester, birthdays and holidays.
dai-2014.found: Searches for 'diet', gym visits and new goal commitments all rose after temporal landmarks. The authors propose that landmarks mark off new 'mental accounting periods' that relegate past failures to a previous period and prompt a big-picture view of one's life.
dai-2014.limits: Observational data about when people start, not whether they succeed or persist; the proposed mechanism was not tested directly in these studies. The samples are internet users, one university's gym members and users of one website.

superville-2014.authors: Superville DJ, Pargament KI, Lee JW
superville-2014.title: Sabbath Keeping and Its Relationships to Health and Well-Being: A Mediational Analysis
superville-2014.journal: International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
superville-2014.design: Survey of 5,411 Seventh-day Adventists in North America, testing four possible pathways (religious coping, religious support, diet and exercise) between Sabbath keeping and physical and mental health, using bootstrapped mediation analysis.
superville-2014.found: Sabbath keeping was associated with better physical and mental health, and each of the four pathways partly explained the link.
superville-2014.limits: Survey data from a single denomination with strong health teaching, so the findings may not generalise; the design cannot show that Sabbath keeping causes better health rather than healthier, more committed people keeping it. Health was self-reported.

proeschold-bell-2022.authors: Proeschold-Bell RJ, Stringfield B, Yao J, Choi J, Eagle D, Hybels CF, Parnell H, Keefe K, Shilling S
proeschold-bell-2022.title: Changes in Sabbath-Keeping and Mental Health Over Time: Evaluation Findings From the Sabbath Living Study
proeschold-bell-2022.design: Longitudinal evaluation of United Methodist clergy who attended Sabbath-keeping workshops: 227 consented and 167 completed the baseline and at least one follow-up survey at 3 and 9 months. No control group.
proeschold-bell-2022.found: Participants reported keeping the Sabbath more often at 3 and 9 months. Those who increased their Sabbath-keeping reported greater personal accomplishment at work; those who decreased it reported worse anxiety, lower spiritual well-being in ministry and less flourishing mental health. Several outcomes, including depersonalisation and relationship quality, showed no association.
proeschold-bell-2022.limits: No control group, a convenience sample of clergy, Sabbath defined by each participant and measured as self-reported frequency, many outcomes tested without correction for multiple comparisons; the authors call it exploratory.

haslam-2006.title: Dehumanization: An Integrative Review
haslam-2006.design: Theoretical and integrative review of research on dehumanisation across social psychology and neighbouring fields.
haslam-2006.found: Proposes that dehumanisation denies people two distinct senses of humanness: the traits that are uniquely human and the traits that make up human nature. Denying the first pictures people as animal-like; denying the second pictures them as objects or machines. Argues that dehumanisation is an everyday social phenomenon rooted in ordinary social thinking, not only something found in extreme conflict.
haslam-2006.limits: A conceptual review and model, not a new study. Later researchers have questioned how often people who harm others truly see them as less than human, rather than as humans they blame, hate or wish to punish.

harris-2006.title: Dehumanizing the Lowest of the Low: Neuroimaging Responses to Extreme Out-Groups
harris-2006.design: Functional brain imaging (fMRI): 10 participants viewed 48 photographs of social groups chosen to represent the four types of the stereotype content model, and 12 participants viewed objects.
harris-2006.found: The medial prefrontal cortex, a region involved in thinking about other people, was active for every social group except the 'extreme' out-groups stereotyped as both hostile and incompetent, such as addicts and homeless people. These groups especially activated the insula and amygdala, a pattern consistent with disgust. The authors conclude that such groups may be perceived as less than human.
harris-2006.limits: Very small samples, and inferring a mental state (seeing someone as less than human) from activity in one brain region is uncertain. An early, influential study that needs larger replications.

kteily-2015.authors: Kteily N, Bruneau E, Waytz A, Cotterill S
kteily-2015.title: The Ascent of Man: Theoretical and Empirical Evidence for Blatant Dehumanization
kteily-2015.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
kteily-2015.design: Seven studies in three countries introducing and validating a blatant measure of dehumanisation, in which people place groups on the familiar 'Ascent of Man' image of evolutionary progress, and comparing it with subtle and implicit measures.
kteily-2015.found: Many people were willing to rate some groups as less evolved. This blatant dehumanisation was more strongly linked to support for social hierarchy than subtle measures, predicted harmful attitudes and behaviour towards several groups beyond ordinary prejudice, was stable over time, and rose sharply after real attacks (the Boston Marathon bombings and the Woolwich attack in England), when it predicted support for torture and retaliatory violence.
kteily-2015.limits: Survey studies, so the links are correlations, not proof that dehumanising causes cruelty. Placing a group on a cartoon of evolution may capture contempt or hostility as much as a literal belief that people are less human.

dunn-2008.authors: Dunn EW, Aknin LB, Norton MI
dunn-2008.title: Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness
dunn-2008.design: Three studies: a nationally representative US survey (cross-sectional), a longitudinal field study of how employees spent a work bonus, and a small experiment in which people were randomly given money and told to spend it on themselves or on others by the end of the day
dunn-2008.found: Spending more of one's income on others predicted greater happiness, both in the survey and in the windfall study; and participants randomly assigned to spend money on others reported greater happiness than those assigned to spend it on themselves.
dunn-2008.limits: The samples, especially in the experiment and the bonus study, were small, as the authors' own later replication report notes of the field generally (n < 100 per group). The survey is correlational. A large preregistered replication (Aknin et al. 2020) found the effect is real in some designs but often much smaller.

aknin-2020.authors: Aknin LB, Dunn EW, Proulx J, Lok I, Norton MI
aknin-2020.title: Does spending money on others promote happiness?: A registered replication report
aknin-2020.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
aknin-2020.design: Three high-powered preregistered experiments: 712 students randomly assigned to buy something for themselves or a stranger in need; 1,950 adults asked to recall spending on themselves or someone else; and a modified recall study with 5,199 participants designed to increase engagement
aknin-2020.found: Students who spent on a stranger in need reported greater momentary happiness. In the first recall study, people who recalled prosocial spending were not happier. In the larger, more engaging recall study, they were happier, but the difference was small.
aknin-2020.limits: Run by the original authors. Happiness was measured immediately and briefly, not over weeks; the effect depends heavily on the method, and the earlier small studies probably overstated its size.

haushofer-2016.title: The Short-term Impact of Unconditional Cash Transfers to the Poor: Experimental Evidence from Kenya
haushofer-2016.design: Randomised controlled trial of unconditional cash transfers by the charity GiveDirectly to poor households in rural Kenya, randomised at village and household level, and within the treatment group by recipient gender, timing (lump sum or monthly) and size (US$404 or US$1,525 PPP)
haushofer-2016.found: Household monthly consumption rose from $158 to $193 PPP nine months after transfers began, and recipients reported large increases in psychological wellbeing. There was no overall effect on the stress hormone cortisol. Monthly transfers improved food security more; lump sums were more often spent on durable goods.
haushofer-2016.limits: Short-term (about nine months) and one region with one charity, so it cannot show long-run effects or what happens when such transfers are scaled up across a whole economy; effects on neighbours who did not receive transfers need separate study.

blood-2001.title: Intensely pleasurable responses to music correlate with activity in brain regions implicated in reward and emotion
blood-2001.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
blood-2001.design: Brain imaging (PET) of cerebral blood flow while listeners heard music they had chosen because it reliably gave them 'shivers down the spine', with heart rate, muscle activity and breathing also recorded.
blood-2001.found: Reports of chills came with changes in heart rate, muscle activity and breathing. As chills grew more intense, blood flow rose or fell in regions involved in reward, emotion and arousal, including the ventral striatum, midbrain, amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex: the same circuitry engaged by food, sex and addictive drugs. The authors conclude that music recruits the brain's ancient pleasure and reward system.
blood-2001.limits: A small, selected sample and a correlational design; PET blood-flow imaging cannot show which brain chemicals are involved. It shows what happens in the brain during intense musical pleasure, not what the experience means.

salimpoor-2011.authors: Salimpoor VN, Benovoy M, Larcher K, Dagher A, Zatorre RJ
salimpoor-2011.title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
salimpoor-2011.design: [11C]raclopride PET to measure dopamine release, plus fMRI with the same listeners and music, together with measures of autonomic arousal; eight participants screened from 217 respondents because they reliably felt chills to music.
salimpoor-2011.found: Dopamine was released in the striatum at the peak of emotional arousal to music. The timing split in two: the caudate was more involved while listeners anticipated the peak, and the nucleus accumbens during the peak itself. Music, an abstract stimulus, engages the same dopamine reward system as tangible rewards.
salimpoor-2011.limits: Only eight participants, chosen because they reliably get chills, so the results may not generalise. It shows the chemistry of musical pleasure, not whether the music is about anything real; the same system responds to food, money and drugs.

martinez-molina-2016.authors: Martínez-Molina N, Mas-Herrero E, Rodríguez-Fornells A, Zatorre RJ, Marco-Pallarés J
martinez-molina-2016.title: Neural correlates of specific musical anhedonia
martinez-molina-2016.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
martinez-molina-2016.design: fMRI in three groups of 15 people with low, average and high sensitivity to musical reward, listening to music and doing a monetary gambling task.
martinez-molina-2016.found: People who get no pleasure from music despite normal hearing ('specific musical anhedonia') showed reduced activity in the nucleus accumbens to music but normal responses to winning money, and weaker connections between the right auditory cortex and the reward system. People unusually sensitive to music showed stronger connections.
martinez-molina-2016.limits: Small groups, a correlational design, and sensitivity measured by questionnaire. It shows that musical pleasure depends on a particular link in the brain that varies between people, which neither proves nor disproves that music can carry meaning.

langlois-2000.authors: Langlois JH, Kalakanis L, Rubenstein AJ, Larson A, Hallam M, Smoot M
langlois-2000.title: Maxims or myths of beauty? A meta-analytic and theoretical review
langlois-2000.design: Meta-analyses of 919 effect sizes drawn from over 1,800 articles, testing three sayings: beauty is in the eye of the beholder, never judge a book by its cover, and beauty is only skin-deep
langlois-2000.found: Raters agreed strongly about who is attractive within a culture (effective reliability about r = .90 for adults rating adults), across ethnic groups (r = .88) and across cultures (r = .94). Attractive children and adults were judged more positively and treated better than unattractive ones (for the treatment of adults, d = 0.54), even by people who knew them, and attractive people also showed somewhat more positive traits and behaviours.
langlois-2000.limits: Effective reliability measures how well the averaged ratings of many judges agree, so it can be high even when individual judges differ a good deal. Most studies used photographs and Western samples, and the data are largely correlational, so they cannot say why attractive people fare better. The review is over twenty years old and did not test for publication bias in the way later meta-analyses do.

vessel-2018.authors: Vessel EA, Maurer N, Denker AH, Starr GG
vessel-2018.title: Stronger shared taste for natural aesthetic domains than for artifacts of human culture
vessel-2018.design: Rating experiments in which participants said how much they liked images from several visual domains (faces, natural landscapes, architecture and artworks), with a second study comparing landscapes and buildings directly; shared taste was measured by how closely each person's ratings matched other people's
vessel-2018.found: Taste for faces and landscapes was largely shared, while taste for architecture and artworks was much more individual. The second study confirmed stronger agreement for natural scenes than for buildings. The authors propose that natural domains matter to everyone in the same way, while human-made things are judged through each person's own experience and knowledge.
vessel-2018.limits: Liking images on a screen is not the same as standing in a building or before a painting, and liking is not the same as judging something beautiful. The study cannot say how much of the shared taste is inborn and how much is shared culture. We took the findings from the abstract and the institute's summary; check sample sizes and statistics in the full paper.

ishizu-2011.title: Toward a brain-based theory of beauty
ishizu-2011.design: Brain-imaging (fMRI) study of 21 people, who rated paintings and pieces of music for beauty on a scale of 1 to 9 while in the scanner
ishizu-2011.found: One region, the medial orbito-frontal cortex, was active when people experienced both visual and musical beauty, and its activity rose with how beautiful they judged the work to be. The authors propose a single 'faculty of beauty' in the brain that does not depend on whether beauty comes through the eyes or the ears.
ishizu-2011.limits: A small sample, and correlation only. The same region is involved in reward and valuing in general, so its activity cannot show what beauty is. The finding fits both the view that beauty is only a brain response and the view that the brain is how we perceive something real.
